newsitem.title: USA: Appeals court rejects NJ display of menorah, creche.
newsitem.headline: Appeals court rejects NJ display of menorah, creche.

text.p: A federal appeals court Monday ruled that Jersey City, N.J., violated the constitutional separation of church and state in a city-sponsored display featuring a Chistian creche and Jewish menorah.

Furthermore, a lower court erred in saying the addition of figurines of Santa Claus, Frosty the Snowman and a red sled did not bring the display into adherance with the constitution, a three-judge panel of the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said in its opinion.

"Jersey City's display of the creche at the seat of City government power impremissibly conveyed a message of government endorsement of religon. And, in our view, the City's addition of Santa, Frosty and a red sled did little to secularise that message," the appeals court said.
The case stems from a 1994 suit by the American Civil Liberties Union, protesting the display of the creche and menorah in front of the Jersey City City Hall -- a three-decade old tradition.
A U.S. District Court forbid the practice in a 1995 ruling. In response, Jersey City that year put up its traditional display with the addition of the Santa, snowman and sled figures.
It also put African-American Kwanzaa symbols on the city's Christmas tree and large signs saying the display was part of a year-round city celebration of ethnic and cultural diversity.

Although the ACLU protested, the district court ruled that the modified display was permissible, saying the city had sufficiently "demystified, desanctifed and deconsecrated" the religous context of the display.
The appeals court disagreed and returned the case to the lower court to be reconsidered.
